title: Coral Castle
summary: A Latvian immigrant spent 28 years carving an elaborate castle from oolite limestone in the Florida heat, working only at night and alone, all for a fiancee who never came to see it.

content.intro: "It's not difficult if you know how." That was the only explanation Edward Leedskalnin ever offered for the impossible thing he built south of Miami. Standing five feet tall and weighing roughly a hundred pounds, this Latvian immigrant single-handedly quarried, carved, and placed over a thousand tons of oolite limestone into a fantastical sculpture garden -- complete with a nine-ton revolving gate so perfectly balanced that a child could push it open with one finger. He worked only at night. He refused all witnesses. And he dedicated the whole monument to a sixteen-year-old girl in Latvia who had called off their wedding the day before the ceremony. She never visited.

sections.title: A Broken Engagement, A Lifelong Obsession
sections.body: Edward Leedskalnin was born in Riga, Latvia, in 1887. At twenty-six, his sixteen-year-old fiancee Agnes Skuvst -- or possibly Hermine Lusis, according to Latvian records -- cancelled their wedding just one day before the ceremony. Leedskalnin emigrated to America, drifted through Canada and Texas, contracted tuberculosis that he claimed magnets helped cure, and eventually landed in Florida City, on the edge of the Everglades. There, at what was then one of the most remote spots in the continental United States, he began quarrying coral rock from the ground beneath his feet. He worked for more than twenty-eight years, always alone, always at night. When asked why he built the castle, he gave the same cryptic answer: it was for his "Sweet Sixteen." In his self-published pamphlet, A Book in Every Home, Leedskalnin hinted that his Sweet Sixteen was more an ideal than any real person. The romantic legend, however, proved far more durable than the clarification.

sections.title: Stone Furniture and Celestial Instruments
sections.body: Despite its name, Coral Castle is not made of coral. The material is oolite -- oolitic limestone -- a sedimentary rock that lies just inches below the topsoil across southeastern Florida. Leedskalnin carved it into an astonishing catalog of objects: a two-story tower that served as his living quarters, a heart-shaped table, a table cut in the shape of Florida, twenty-five rocking chairs, crescent-moon seats, a bathtub, beds, a throne, a barbecue, a water well, and a working fountain. He built an accurate sundial and a polar telescope aligned with the North Star. He raised an obelisk. The perimeter walls stand eight feet tall, fitted together without mortar, with joints so precise that no light passes between them. Most objects are carved from single blocks averaging several tons each.

sections.title: The Nine-Ton Gate
sections.body: The most famous feature of the castle is its revolving gate -- an eight-foot-tall slab of oolite that once swung with almost no effort. For decades, the gate's effortless rotation baffled visitors. When it finally stopped working in 1986, it took six men and a crane to remove it. Inside, engineers found Leedskalnin's secret: he had drilled a vertical shaft from top to bottom and inserted a metal rod that rested on a salvaged truck bearing. The stone balanced on that single point. When the bearing rusted out, the magic stopped. It was repaired and reinstalled on July 23, 1986, and failed again in 2005. After a second repair, the gate still turns, but not with the supernatural ease it once had. The engineering was clever, not mystical -- but Leedskalnin preferred the mystery.

sections.title: Moving Day
sections.body: Around 1936, when development threatened to encroach on his privacy in Florida City, Leedskalnin decided to relocate -- and he took the entire castle with him. He hired a truck and driver to haul the carved stones ten miles north to a site outside Homestead, but he loaded and unloaded every block himself, always insisting that the driver look away. The move took three years. At his new location, which he named "Rock Gate" after the massive rear swinging gate, Leedskalnin quarried additional oolite from the ground just feet from the walls. The two pools and pits beside the southern wall are the quarries themselves. He charged visitors twenty-five cents for a tour -- but let anyone in free who could not pay. When the bell at the front gate rang twice, he would descend from his tower and walk his guests through every room.

sections.title: Going to the Hospital
sections.body: In November 1951, Leedskalnin fell ill. He hung a handwritten sign on the front gate -- "Going to the Hospital" -- and rode the bus to Jackson Memorial Hospital in Miami. He suffered a stroke and died twenty-eight days later of kidney failure at the age of sixty-four. His nephew inherited the property but soon sold it to Julius Levin, a retired Chicago jeweler, who turned it into a full tourist attraction and renamed it from Rock Gate to Coral Castle. In 1984, the property was listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Today, Coral Castle draws visitors who come to marvel at its impossible-seeming engineering and to hear one man's answer to heartbreak: a castle carved from the bones of Florida, one stone at a time, in the dark.

content.flightContext: Coral Castle sits at 25.50N, 80.44W in unincorporated Miami-Dade County near Homestead, Florida, along South Dixie Highway (US-1). From the air, the compound is small and easily lost in suburban sprawl -- look for the stone walls just west of US-1 between Florida City and Leisure City. Homestead Air Reserve Base (KHST) lies approximately 5 miles to the east. Miami International Airport (KMIA) is 35 miles north. The Everglades spread to the west, and the Florida Keys begin about 25 miles south. Terrain is dead flat limestone barely above sea level. Recommended viewing altitude: 2,000-3,000 feet AGL for context of the surrounding area.
